subtopic: REPORTED LAYOFFS AT ELDORADO REFINERY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED LAYOFFS AT ELDORADO REFINERY
speechtext:
I
should like to direct a question to the Minister of Defence Production, now the Acting Prime Minister. Will the minister give the house a statement concerning the reported layoff at the Eldorado Mining and Refining company plant at Port Hope? Will the minister tell us also whether further layoffs are contemplated, and if so where the uranium mined in Canada is to be processed?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REPORTED LAYOFFS AT ELDORADO REFINERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a telephone call was received in my office requesting this information, and I tried to reach the president of the company but found that he was in the Northwest Territories. The facts as I have them are that the fire which destroyed the mill at Port Radium is primarily responsible. The mill which was burnt was an old mill designed chiefly for the recovery of radium ore. Since the fire it has been replaced by a more modern mill which gives a greater degree of concentration of the uranium recovered. This means there is a smaller tonnage of ore to be treated at Port Hope, and therefore instead of a three-shift operation the refinery will, in the future, operate on a two-shift basis.
A further factor is that part of the staff at Port Hope were engaged in experimental work in designing a new refinery. It has been decided to defer the building of a new refinery for the time being. The staff engaged in that particular problem, numbering some ten or twelve, has been dispensed with. The employment, as of July 31, which was the peak employment, was 227 people. At present there are 199 people, and on December 15, when it is expected the two-shift operation will commence, employment will be between 150 and 160 people.
In answer to the second part of the question, I might say that all the uranium that is being mined in Canada is being refined at Port Hope.

When speaking in the house yesterday, and as recorded at page 73 of Hansard, the hon member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) had this to say:
It becomes clear from the speech of the leader of the official opposition and the speech of the leader of the Social Credit party that today the C.C.F. is the only party in this house which is prepared at this session to support legislation for the inauguration of a national health insurance program.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for York South completely misunderstood the
102	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Shaw
hon. member for Peace River <Mr. Low) when he outlined our position with respect to health insurance. Had my leader been opposed to a scheme of national health insurance, surely he would not have proceeded to envision the type of health insurance scheme which we would conceive of.
What the hon. member for Peace River asserted was that we are in favour of a national health insurance scheme, to commence at the earliest possible time; but he cautioned the house against any overeager effort on the part of anyone to catapult this nation or the state into any comprehensive scheme of health insurance or hospitalization before the means are available or the facilities are ready for it. The Social Credit leader indicated that the kind of health insurance scheme which we envision would first ensure that we have sufficient doctors, dentists, technicians, clinics and hospital beds available in order to provide the services for all our people under a national health insurance scheme.
The hon. member for Peace River then went on to list what he considered to be five essential features to be embodied in any national health insurance scheme. They were, first, that we have a fair measure of individual responsibility; second, that the patients will be guaranteed the right to have their choice of doctors and that the program must guarantee that there will be no regimentation of patients, doctors, nurses and hospitals; third, that emphasis must be placed upon preventive medicine or, in other words, keeping the people well; fourth, joint co-operation on the municipal, provincial and federal levels, with administration by the municipalities and the provincial governments working in co-operation; and then finally, provincial and federal subsidies to keep costs down.
Such a stand, Mr. Speaker, does not represent opposition to the establishment or the inauguration of a national health insurance program at this session. What we are opposed to, as my leader stated, is being catapulted holus-bolus into a complete scheme where we have not the necessary facilities in order to guarantee the services to our people. But surely a step can be taken now, along with steps that have already been taken, to establish health services with the idea in mind that this is a part of a national health insurance scheme. We say that this represents a common-sense, practical approach to this extremely important proposition. I hope it will not be said again that we are opposed to the inauguration of a national health insurance scheme at this session.
During this debate several hon. members who have spoken have made reference to agriculture and the present position of agriculture in our national economy. I hope to devote only a few moments to this subject, because I do desire to bring before the house one important matter which I think is deserving of immediate and serious consideration. It is true-and I have said this here upon many	occasions-that	my constituency
embraces one of the finest mixed farming areas in Canada. The livestock produced in that area, along with other farm products, have been consistent winners at fairs in this country. That is a fact which testifies, of course, to the excellence of the agricultural products which are produced in that area. More than one world title has gone to the Red Deer area.
We all know, especially when we live in a mixed farming area of that kind, that livestock prices, in the main, determine the degree of stability or instability of the basic industry. Last spring, as I pointed out in this house, the closed markets resulting from foot-and-mouth disease had a most disastrous effect upon livestock producers in that area, especially upon those who were feeding cattle and preparing them for the markets. The existing floor prices for hogs and for cattle, quoted invariably f.o.b. some other place except that where the commodities are produced, leave much to be desired as far as our agriculture is concerned. Apart from the most exceptional cases, the floor prices for those products are absolutely meaningless as far as our producers are concerned. All one has to do is to examine the returns which the farmers are receiving for cattle and hogs. Too frequently-and I feel it necessary to mention this matter-the cost-conscious tax-burdened consuming public regard excessive resale prices for farm products as an indication of undue profits accruing to the farmers iand what they would think to be a generally prosperous agriculture.
It is my conviction, Mr. Speaker, that the consuming public should be made to understand that, despite high resale prices for farm products, the net position of the farmer today, under excessive production costs, leaves a good deal to be desired and leaves the agricultural industry-especially that aspect of it relating to livestock production-in a precarious position in many instances.
In my estimation price spreads should be the major concern of any government, and every government should make every effort to find out the facts, to make those facts
FMr. Shaw.]

known to the public, and in short to interpret the position of the farmer to the consuming public of this country.

speechtext:
Yes, accurately, as the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) interjects.
With regard to agriculture and matters relative thereto, I should like to devote just a moment to the question of prairie farm assistance, particularly as prairie farm assistance applies to an area such as mine where farmers do not qualify as a consequence of crop losses resulting from drought but rather as a consequence of crop losses resulting from hail. In 1951 disastrous hail storms swept across that area. Losses were heavy. For almost the first time in thirteen years, during which time the farmers have been compelled to pay into the fund under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, they looked to the P.F.A.A. for some compensation as a consequence of those losses. One of the first things we learned, Mr. Speaker, was that the P.F.A.A. was originally designed to take care of crop losses resulting from drought. The same regulations are carried forward today, in the main, and the endeavour is made to apply them to hail areas. As a result, the act becomes almost impossible of administration, and the unfairness which develops as a consequence is causing the farmers of my area to charge the government with the rankest kind of discrimination. I am telling the house only exactly what the farmers themselves are saying. Regardless of their politics, in every part of that area they are issuing that charge.
I should like to underline the fact, Mr. Speaker, that for twelve to thirteen years those farmers have been paying one per cent of the price on all grains which have been marketed, through the recognized channels of marketing, of course. In the first place, I should like to know why with respect to an area such as the Red Deer area, where actually little wheat is grown, the main crops being coarse grains, they should persist in using wheat as the grain to determine eligibility. In the second place, in contrast to drought, hail cuts narrow swaths through the area. Hail will hop, skip and jump through an area. In a good area where production is so heavy, where hail does not strike, it is virtually impossible for 60 per cent of the farmers to qualify, because part of that township can be devastated, but because production is so high in the other part of the area it brings the average up above that which is used to exclude the township.
The Address-Mr. Shaw
In the third place, the six section block which must exist, the block in which production is less than eight bushels to the acre, is unreasonable and altogether too high as far as hail is concerned.
When farmers proposed that the unit of eligibility be lowered below the six-section block they were told that it would encourage poor farming. Poor farming has been encouraged in the dried-out areas ever since this act came into effect. The farmers in my area claim that there is no reason in the world why the unit of eligibility under P.F.A.A. in relation to hail should not be reduced at least to the one-section basis.
The farmers have indicated to me that they are willing to pay more than the one per cent; but if they are going to pay they would like to be in a position where they would have a reasonable chance to qualify under the act. We find situations like these. I think of one where twelve sections in a solid block were hailed out a hundred per cent. They paid P.F.A. on sections one to eleven. Section twelve was part of the block that was hailed out a hundred per cent, but because they are able to drag it in with five other sections alongside of an ineligible township, they excluded the area wholly and completely, leaving those farmers with devastated crops but yet not a cent available under the act.
There is another aspect of this which is causing quite some concern. While farmers with 100 acres to 200 acres under cultivation lose everything as a consequence of hail and get nothing from P.F.A., yet we find a policy under which the government will pay a $200 flat award on farms where the actual acreage under cultivation is less than 25, categorizing such farms as a farm in the development stage. I have no objection to these farmers getting $200, since they paid for it, but it is hard to reconcile that with the situation where farmers lose 200 acres of grain and qualify for absolutely nothing. I am not criticizing the inspectors; I am not criticizing the men in the district offices who administer P.F.A.A. They are trying to do the best possible job with an act that is, as I said before, almost impossible of administration, if you want justice, equity and fairness, and the absolute removal of anything which appears to be discriminatory in character.
Let me point out that this has caused a lot of criticism. It has caused a lot of unhappiness. In my view, this act should be referred to the agriculture committee and a complete study should be made of P.F.A.A. in relation to hail, because, and I repeat, the regulations, originally designed to compensate

The Address-Mr. Shaw farmers who had lost their crops as a consequence of drought, do not make sense when they are applied to these hailed-out areas.
During this debate, Mr. Speaker, considerable attention has been given to national defence. It is to national defence and defence production that I desire to devote my attention for a while. We Social Crediters have been wholly conscious at all times of the grave dangers confronting this nation. As a consequence of that, we have supported appropriations for defence. When these estimates have come before the house we have invariably questioned and sought information, and we have supported what the government considers to be essential appropriations for national defence. We are absolutely convinced that Canadians are fully prepared to bear whatever burden is necessary in order to ensure that we shall have the best possible and most adequate defences.
We have also supported the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the provisions made by this parliament for Canada's share of the costs of NATO. We have gone considerably farther than any other group in this house in urging compulsory service in Canada's home defence units, and we have at all times urged the establishment of realistic trade practices to strengthen Canada economically and to strengthen the commonwealth. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think we have displayed through our actions that we have supported and that we will support all appropriations, as I said before, even though they may appear to be burdens, which are necessary in order to provide adequate defences. The Canadian taxpayers, however, demand one thing of us as a parliament. They demand that we give the very closest consideration to every item of defence expenditure, and that we make every conceivable effort to see to it that we are getting our money's worth out of every dollar spent in defence.
I know that during the last session of parliament this house set up a defence expenditures committee. We supported that action because we believed that such was necessary. It was said last year that the purpose of that committee was to try to effect economies consistent with the execution of policies decided by the government. It was under the able chairmanship of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), and although I was not a member of that committee I personally feel that he conducted himself as chairman in commendable fashion.
Between April 8 and June 12 that committee held eighteen meetings. That was a very short period of time, it is true. During the period from April 8 to June 12 the committee, so my reading indicates to me, examined into

government policy as far as defence expenditures were concerned. I noticed in reading all the reports that they gave consideration to control and accounting of materials and stores in the Department of National Defence. I also noticed that they gave consideration to write-off procedure which is followed by the government, including the write-offs resulting from theft, fire and other causes. The committee considered defence orders which had been placed between 1950 and 1952.
They gave consideration to military functions, economies and the possibility of alternative sources of supply. I believe they delved into the naval shipbuilding program. They also gave consideration to the requirements of the army, the navy and the air force. And then, shortly before the committee concluded its deliberations, the construction program of the Department of National Defence, as carried out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and Defence Construction Limited, was given some consideration. As a matter of fact, Mr. D. B. Mansur, president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, did, I understand, make a statement to the committee.
Apparently the committee's deliberations concluded following its consideration of policy and procedure relative to the defence construction program. In my estimation the most important work they have to do is ahead of them. I was very pleased to note that the defence expenditures committee is to be reconstituted. I am going to make several recommendations to the committee that it may, when it is reconstituted, take into consideration.
The first is that I think it has given reasonable consideration to policy; now I think it should devote its attention to the practical application of that policy in the field. And it is in that respect, as I said a moment ago, that I have a few things to say. Let me point out in passing that much consideration has been given to the procurement of such things as uniforms, and it has been said that too many of this have been bought or too much of that. Well, that does not concern me particularly at the moment. I well recall that I was one of those who levelled rather severe criticism at the government back in the early forties for being so wholly unprepared when war broke out. I realize it is most difficult to say that we need just exactly this number of that commodity or that number of another commodity. I say: within reasonable limits let us make sure we have enough to meet any emergency which may suddenly come upon us. I hope we will not be unmindful

of the probability that such an emergency could be only hours away. Let us hope it is much farther away than that.
My personal conviction, one based upon a good deal of personal investigation, is that the defence expenditures committee should be instructed, or that by resolution it should instruct itself. To be more specific, I would suggest that the committee resolve to pick out one particular military establishment in Canada and examine carefully into every aspect of construction relative thereto.
To be even more specific I might go so far as to suggest that they take an establishment within my own constituency, that at Penhold -although I would not want any investigation to be limited to that air station alone. I am going to give one or two reasons why I think such an investigation should be undertaken. First, there is ample evidence-and I witnessed it over a period of months prior to coming down here to Ottawa-of growing public concern and indignation over some of the things that are going on at Penhold. Information came to me; I did not go seeking it until so much of it had come to me that I considered it essential in the public interest to satisfy myself about some of these things.
Needless to say I became absolutely convinced that the defence expenditures committee should carry out an investigation. To be even more specific, I am not satisfied at all with respect to the construction of housing for airmen at some of these establishments. I shall leave Penhold for a moment and come to Namao, in the Edmonton district, where approximately 250 houses are under construction. So far as I know there is no evidence that adequate inspection has been carried out continuously, so far as that project is concerned. There is every evidence for me to believe certain things-and I suggest the committee should ascertain the facts, first of all, about the foundations of these buildings.
On the basis of my own investigations, I feel the contractors have not carried out the specifications as laid down in the contracts.

speechtext: That is not peculiar.

speechtext:
Foundations are run sloppy, as we say. The tamping of concrete has been at an absolute minimum, and footings have been poured on loose backfill, with the obvious result that the foundations cracked and the buildings have settled until all one has to do is go up to them and place a level on the side to discover whether they are plumb or not.
There is reason to believe that green lumber has been used extensively by the contractors, with consequent shrinkage following 68108-8
The Address-Mr. Shaw the application of heat to those buildings, and that cracking in the finish has been general.
There is evidence to believe that the lumber used for framing is of a very inferior quality. It is warped, knotted and checked. So far as those houses are concerned, I suggest the committee should find out whether or not the joists were doubled, as per specifications. I would like the committee to find whether the chimney wells were doubled as per specifications, and whether the bridging of joists was carried out according to specifications.
I would like to know where the nails were that are presumed to have been used in a building that has to stand for any length of time.
So far as the general framing is concerned, the materials are highly questionable, again. The prefabricated wall sections have been left outside, some of them as far back as last winter, and have warped. Nailing appears to be at a minimum, and partition girths are hanging by nails having been driven up from underneath, again not according to specifications.
I would like the committee to look into these cracked walls, and to find out whether the inside studding has been carried out according to specifications. I would like to know whether or not in some of these buildings the centres are sixteen inches, according to specifications, or whether they are forty-eight inches. I think, too, that the single plates on the partitions are not continuous throughout.
I am not going to continue enumerating all these individual items so far as that particular station is concerned. However, I have scores upon scores of them I would be quite willing to make available to the committee. And, oh yes, I would like to know how the hardwood flooring has been put on, whether it was placed crosswise in some of the halls, or carried out according to specifications. I would ask the committee to examine the floors and see to what extent they are blocked up to the sole plates, in respect of both the exterior and the interior walls.
I should like to know whether lime mortar has been used in these chimneys or whether cement mortar was used as provided for by the specifications. I should also like the committee to find out in how many cases lime mortar froze before it was ever used. I should like the committee to examine the basement floors to see whether they were steel trowelled or whether they were properly dry finished as per specifications. I should like to know also whether these buildings all have the number of windows called for by the specifications.
On top of all this I think the committee should find out how many change orders were

The Address-Mr. Shaw issued alter the buildings were under construction. I should like to know if the change orders were carried out as per specifications and what additional amounts were paid to the contractors as a result of those change orders. I should like to know how many of those change orders were absolutely essential.
I think if the committee is to look into these things it should call in the inspectors who have been connected with this job. Not only should the committee call in inspectors who are presently on the job; it is quite conceivable it might be wise to call in inspectors who are no longer on the job.
I indicated a moment ago that I should like to see the committee go to Penhold. These things are causing consternation among the people. There are some questions which should be answered. First I should like to find out something which has to do with construction only indirectly. I should like to know what it has cost the Canadian taxpayer as a consequence of the R.C.A.F. moving families out to that area before the houses for their accommodation were even nearly completed. What allowances have been paid to airmen to house their families in an area where it is difficult to procure civilian housing, a condition which has been so for a long period of time. I should like to know what additional costs have been involved and why these families were moved from where they were quartered when they were.
With regard to heating, I should like to know the exact cost of installing the temporary heating system which was operated with boilers brought in from New York. What extra amounts have been paid to the prime contractor as a consequence of installing the temporary heating system I should like to find out also what is involved in the establishment of an overhead heating system which has never been used and which according to my information will never be used because it is intended to have a central underground heating system. We should find out the why and wherefore of this heating.
Here is another thing the committee should look into. They built some pretty good roads at Penhold. They went down as I think they should have, they scarified the surface, they moved in new dirt and spent a lot of money constructing roads with the exception of putting on a hard surface. But then they came along to instal the water and steam distribution system and their sewage system. In doing this they just cut crisscross over the roads which had just been built. Why should a thing of that sort occur? Was there a lack of co-ordination or planning? What is the reason?
People in my area are asking me why trucks moved in 48-inch cement culverts, pounding down the road with them day after day, and then turned right around, hauled them out and then hauled in 24-inch culverts. That is something that should be looked into. These were to be used for storm sewers, I presume on the runway, although I am not too certain of that.
I want to know above all else what provision is being made to repay to the Canadian taxpayers money saved by contractors who are using R.C.A.F. equipment in carrying out their contracts, who are using draglines, bulldozers, et cetera, belonging to the R.C.A.F. I should like to know if proper deductions have been made for the use of that equipment which, as I say, belongs to the Royal Canadian Air Force. There is evidence that several contractors are using government equipment in order to carry out contracts which they have entered into.
I think the committee should find out about the lighting arrangements. Is there a bulk contract with the power company, or are meters used? I have reason to believe that they are operating on meters. If they are, and I say "if they are", it must be costing the Canadian taxpayer a pretty sum because thousands of powerful lights are going day after day and night after night, in the hangars and out of the hangars, when the station is not even operating. This was true up to two weeks ago. If they are operating on meters, I should like to know what the committee thinks about that. If they are not operating on meters we should be told something of the bulk contract, if such exists.
Then about water. I am informed that International Water Wells have been in there ever since last spring. People have come to me and asked whether they were drilling for oil. Penhold was operated as an air station during the last war and adequate amounts of water were secured at depths of 150 to 200 feet to carry out the training scheme at that time. I would say that that would be adequate for any scheme which might be inaugurated at this time. I should like to know the amount and nature of the contract with International Water Wells because, as I say, they seem to be just playing around there. They could have got a lot more done if they had been drilling for oil. Let me re-emphasize that there are wells producing abundant water from 150, 175 and 200 feet, and have been right along.
The fuel contract has caused some people a good deal of concern and I think it should be examined into. The supply contract does not concern me quite so much as the handling contract. I should like to know how many times the coal is handled and I should like

to know the details o f the contract each handler has. I should like to know whether the amount paid to the final handler, as it were, is considerably in excess of what is paid at other stations. I should like to know also whether that contractor is ever around the station or did he simply let a subcontract and do very well as a consequence. I have no grievance as far as the individuals are concerned; it is simply a matter of practice and policy.
I assume that my time is almost exhausted but I do want to conclude by saying that during last summer and early fall a great many people came to me. I did not go out seeking anything. These taxpayers began to express concern and I deemed it my duty to try to find out a few things. I am disturbed and people are disturbed. If everything is all right, then I think it necessary that we find that out through a properly constituted method of examination. I know that there have been denials, but that does not surprise me because when I charged in 1945 that there was wanton destruction of surplus war material at Pen-hold I was confronted with vehement denials from all quarters. In fact, on the floor of this house my charges were denied and everything was done to discourage me. However, it so happened that I was a member of the war expenditures and economies committee at that time, and after a great many weeks and a great deal of cross-examination we were given the frank admission that the charges were absolutely true and the committee recommended a change of policy relative thereto. Therefore I am never too greatly impressed by blanket denials. I know the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) cannot be on each one of these jobs but I do say we should be able to acquire a sufficient number of properly qualified inspectors with the right to do their jobs without being hampered, and that they should be allowed to go in there and see that these contracts are carried out as they should be carried out and that the materials that are being used are materials which are essential to the construction of permanent establishments.
It is my understanding that these are to be permanent establishments, and who knows but what the cold war may carry on for twenty-five years or forever, as far as that goes, although we hope not. It is my understanding that they are trying to bring an element of permanency into the construction of these establishments. After all, we are faced with an emergency. We know that. But Canada is not being attacked and it is not as if we were required to put only half the necessary number of nails into a building to get it done in a hurry so that we could drive the enemy back from our shores.
The Address-Mr. Larson
The Canadian taxpayers will bear the burden. They have indicated their willingness to bear the burden of defence no matter what it may be but they require that every conceivable effort be made to ensure that the money which is taken from them and spent is spent in such a way that the results will be obtained which they hope will be achieved, and within a reasonably short period of time. I hope that the government will see fit to recommend to the defence expenditures committee that it should look into these matters or that the committee will take it upon itself to do so. I am sure the taxpayers of Canada will be greatly relieved if they know that that is going to be done.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that, the practice having been established in this house some time ago, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Deslieres) and the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) should be congratulated on their efforts in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Having been subjected to the same pressures at one time, I feel that probably I realize, more than is generally the case, the excellence of their speeches made under such pressures.
Looking at our national picture at this time in the life of this government I would say that the keynote of the government's activities has been a sort of gathering up of the loose ends that have resulted from the pressures exerted on our national unity and the building of this country once again and forever into one solid unit. Geographically, as I have said before in the house, we are split by miles and miles of area separating the various portions of the country one from the other, and it is very easy for us to drift into a position where we are sectional in our outlook. With the various sectional appeals that have been made to different groups in this country in the past by other governments, I do not feel that any other government would have the ability to continue moulding this country into one national unit as our present government has done.
In Saskatchewan we recently had a little contest about who was going to run that province, and the party which might form an alternative government at some time in this country was so short of candidates that I do not see how it could ever feel that it could form an alternative government to the one in power today.

Yes, but we at least tried. The present government, in conformity with the policy of building up the national unity of

The Address-Mr. Larson the country, has carried out a social welfare and security policy which I think-and I think I will meet with agreement-is second to none in the world. It was felt by many of us that after our senior citizens had served their time in adding to our economic welfare they should receive compensation as of right for their services, and hence the old age pension without a means test. It was also realized by the present government that it was most necessary to foster the interests of our greatest asset, the youth of the country. In some cases it was thought that they were not receiving as much of our national wealth as they should and under our family allowance system mothers were given a bonus according to the number of their children.
It was thought by the government that workers who, for certain reasons, could not obtain employment should have some sort of insurance against unemployment-hence unemployment insurance. Large numbers of people throughout the country and among the representation in the House of Commons are asking for a health insurance scheme. I have lived under a health insurance scheme most of my life provided by our own municipal doctor and hospital set-up, and a good many other rural municipalities in my part of the country have done the same thing. We found that it worked very well and up until the time the health system was put on a provincial basis we seemed to be getting along quite well in my part of the country.
I am certainly in favour of a national health insurance scheme, but one fact that I think we should look at is that there have been national health insurance schemes in many other countries. I do not think anybody will debate the question very strongly with me when I say that the roadblock in the dollar-sterling relationship may be caused to quite some extent by the health scheme put into effect in Great Britain under the labour movement. I think we should examine that situation very carefully because as a nation we certainly do not want to get ourselves into the position where we start something that is not on a sound basis and which we cannot carry out.
The province of Saskatchewan, where I live, has established a provincial hospitalization plan. It was thought that it could be carried on through the contribution by each family of a certain amount of money. It was found that not even half of the cost could be paid for by such contributions and a good deal of money had to be taken out of the consolidated revenues of the province in order to continue the system. The health unit that has been set up in Swift Current is one that has been mentioned in this house. The
way the new constituency of Kindersley has been established, the health unit in Swift Current will become in the future one of my direct interests, and I have made some inquiries about it. It involves a large number of doctors. Some years ago the government of Saskatchewan set up a scale, which has been revised from time to time, of doctors' charges, and the top of that scale is considered to be one hundred per cent. Doctors who are doing certain work in cancer research, tuberculosis research and other types of research have had their fee set at three-quarters of the one hundred per cent or seventy-five per cent.
In the Swift Current health unit, the scale of fees as set up by the province partly applies, along with several other deductions, changes and alterations, and the fees for purposes of medical services in that unit have been set at fifty-three per cent of what the government of Saskatchewan considers should be one hundred per cent.
Now, when you consider that doctors are also looking after old age pensioners on a very reduced basis, it appears to me that this system, which has been so highly lauded by various people, is being supported mainly by the doctors themselves. A doctor, like anyone else, has to make a living. If health schemes are going to be supported chiefly by these men who have spent so much time in training, and who should be in the position to make themselves comparatively well off, it seems to me we are asking a great deal of them. When I hear about medical services not being available to people who cannot afford them, I feel like saying that I do not know of a single instance in which a Canadian doctor has ever said to a person, "I will not give my services to you because you cannot pay for them."
All these measures that I have mentioned are actually measures which tend towards welding this country into one national unit. Some people say that perhaps it is time for a change. I believe we should consider what the alternative would be; I think that is a very important consideration, and I believe the people of Canada will consider it very carefully.
Another problem which we have in Canada is our international responsibilities. We joined wholeheartedly in originating the United Nations, and we have closely supported that organization during the whole of its existence. I feel that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), who has had such great honours conferred upon him recently, is correct when he says that the United Nations is still the chief hope for peace. However, we, as well as the people who live behind the iron curtain, did not feel

that we could trust our future to a parliament of the world such as the United Nations could have been. The reason for that is that there are too many people, who might be termed rather irresponsible, controlling a lot of votes in that organization. It was for that reason the security council, with the power of veto, was set up by the big five.
This move, brought about by apprehension in many quarters, practically took the teeth out of the United Nations and hampered its ability to make decisions that would be effective and binding. An armaments buildup was taking place behind the iron curtain, and our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in common with other men who worked closely in designing methods of preventing war, felt that legally we were quite entitled to set up a defence organization within the United Nations. Hence, we have NATO. Now, Canada's responsibilities under NATO are quite extensive. Every day we see criticism levelled at that very much overworked and very responsible minister, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). He is doing a job which, in times past, has required two or three ministers. It is only recently that he has been given an associate minister to help him with that job.
We find absolutely little criticism-we have charges levelled in the house by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw)-of the expenditure of the entire amount of our national revenue. I am speaking percentagewise. There have been the small disappearances in places like Petawawa which have been brought up. We have never had levelled at this government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) or the Minister of National Defence, any charge that could be made stick that there was any amount of fraud or money being diverted into somebody's pocket when it should have been diverted into the channels for which it was intended.
We are going to hear a lot as we go on from various people who feel that we should put the effort we are putting into our NATO commitments into sending food to Asiatic countries. I agree that there is possibly some merit in what they say, but I want to make one point clear. There is absolutely no foundation for the thought that you can stop people from becoming communists by feeding them. For one thing, the job of feeding them is impossible, and communism is not a solution for service. Communism is a materialistic religion which requires of those people who live under its domination worship of the state. The main reason that we will have nothing to do with communism is that we feel we can worship a higher power which is above the state. For that reason all parties
The Address-Mr. Larson in this house have committed themselves to checking that particular phase of life in some of the misled peoples of this world.
The national unity, which I was discussing, depends a good deal on providing satisfaction for the problems which have to be solved in every part of the world as much as in the various parts of this country that are split up by such wide geographical differences. Let us consider some of the things that affect the prairies, because that is the part of the country I represent. The first thing on which I wish to congratulate this government is the operation of the wheat board. I hope that the pressures that are being put on the wheat board from different angles to get higher prices, to do this or that differently, do not affect too seriously the thinking of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because I feel that people generally

even though we have some kickers-are one hundred per cent behind the board.
For another thing, it is easy for me as a farmer to say that I should have this, that I should have that and that I should have something else; but it would be much harder for me as a farmer if I were given the responsibility to go out and get it. I think that people throughout this country agree with me that in the person of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) we have the best "getter" handling our wheat problems at the present time. I hope that he will not take too seriously some of the criticism that is being levelled at him. I agree that we should get the most that we can for our wheat, but I also agree that we are being well served by those who are at present handling the western wheat crop.
There is one other matter I wish to mention, and I have discussed it before. It is something which my people, consisting mostly of farmers and small businessmen, have asked me to bring up for consideration in the House of Commons. I sympathize completely with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) in the task that he has before him because nobody can be popular and collect taxes. I also want to put one thing on the record, and that is that the farmers of Saskatchewan do not mind paying taxes. When the farmers of Saskatchewan know that their tax money is being spent in the efficient way it is being spent by this government, there is on their part no more reticence to pay taxes than there is on the part of any other group in this country. None of us likes to pay taxes. However, there is no greater reticence on the part of the farmers of Saskatchewan to pay their fair share of what is required to carry out our national responsibility than there is on the part of any other group in Canada.

The Address-Mr. Larson
But there is one matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue and it is not a criticism of him. It is merely a wish that some sort of system could be evolved so that these people might pay their fair share without having to go through this business of having to keep records. A farmer must keep a certain number of records in order to know where he stands; but, on a small farm, to keep the detailed records that are required properly to make out an income tax return involves a tremendous amount of work and, I might say, annoyance on the part of the farmer and the small businessman. I strongly urge that some formula be worked out-possibly a production tax or some other method of assessment- whereby those people could pay their fair share of the money that they need to pay without having to go into this business of trying to be farmers and accountants all at the same time.
There is only one other matter which I should like to discuss, and it should interest my Social Credit friends. I lived in Calgary when the founder of that party was operating at his peak and when his government was elected in Alberta. He was absolutely insistent that the credit of the country be controlled by the people of the country. He was not the only one who felt that way about the matter. As a result a Liberal government has set up the central bank, and the central bank has, within its powers, that of bolstering credit, if credit needs to be bolstered, or of drawing in credit if a boom or something of that kind is going too wild in this country.

I think we may welcome that fact because, with the end of this parliament there will end, I think, the worst situation that has existed in the House of Commons since confederation.

In the course of the life of this parliament extending over the past three and a half years we have witnessed a decline in the position of the private member on the government side-yes, an end of all pretence of independence; and as to the government, we have seen them waxing ever more and more arrogant, smug and stiff-necked. Bureaucracy is still written all over their attitudes; and if evidences of repentance are to be forthcoming now, assuredly they come too late to be convincing.
I shall have some observations to make on some of the speeches which have been contributed to this debate, particularly that contributed by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). But I wish to say this, and say it fairly and frankly, that the long speech which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)
[Mr. Larson.)


The Address-Mr. Fleming
delivered in this house on Monday is I think by far the weakest speech that any of us ever heard him deliver.
I hope there will be an opportunity to examine some of the things that the Prime Minister had to say in trying to defend the action of his government in levying exorbitant and extortionate taxation and defending those enormous expenditures, and at the same time, after a speech of two and a quarter hours, still found it possible to be utterly silent on two matters that had engaged the attention of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) at some length in his speech, namely, the policy of the government on television, and the matter of health insurance. It certainly was not for lack of time that the Prime Minister did not say a word about either of those subjects. The oversight could not have been unintentional; it can only be inferred, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister ran away from these two subjects.
In 1949 we saw this house assemble. The government, with the largest majority in this house that any government has ever had since confederation, had unrivalled opportunities to solve all the problems of the country. What do we find three and a half years later? We And, sir, that the problems facing this country are greater by far than they were in 1949. This great opportunity that was given to the government to address itself effectively and courageously to meeting Canadian problems has been wasted by this government. These past three and a half years will go down in history as the wasted years. And now we are told that this government is to ask for another chance. In the face of a record like that, of wasted years and lost opportunities, Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied the people of this country will think very carefully before giving another chance to this government to perpetrate another failure.
Sir, the subject of taxation may well engage the attention of this house, because this country is suffering-and that means the vast majority of Canadians in every walk of life -from crushing taxation at the hands of a government that seems to care very little about the burdens that they are imposing upon the people. You see that cavalier attitude reflected in the speech of the Prime Minister on Monday when he said: "I do not think there has been any overtaxation." That is the statement of the Prime Minister, and I presume that is the position upon which his followers are prepared to face the electors, that there has been no overtaxation. Is that not reminiscent of the words used by the Prime Minister in this house on March 6 last, when he attempted to answer the charge
of the Leader of the Opposition that, as revenues and expenditures for the current year then stood, the government had overtaxed every Canadian family-not just taxed, overtaxed-by the sum of $250. The Prime Minister warmed to his task and defended that rate of overtaxation, because he said it was a good thing for the Canadian people that they should be relieved of that surplus purchasing power.
It was a good thing for the Canadian people, so ran his words and his thought, to relieve them of that embarrassing surplus purchasing power. Well, relieve the Canadian people of that surplus purchasing power the government certainly did, and apparently they are quite unrepentant after having deprived the Canadian people of their earnings at a time when the cost of living was high, at a time when most Canadian families were having very great difficulty in making ends meet. The Prime Minister found satisfaction in the extent to which the people were relieved of their means.
And then, of course, while I do not wish to spend too long on the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault), in his very interesting speech last evening, displaying all the helter-skelter zeal of the political convert, he spent no less than half an hour endeavouring to prove that a reduction in taxation is impossible without, so he intimated, following the communist line.
I say in all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, let us have more of these speeches, of the kind made by the Prime Minister when he said that there has been no overtaxation, more of the kind contributed by the hon. member for Bonaventure last evening, because certainly these hon. gentlemen, when the budget comes down in March, are going to have to eat their words; otherwise, it is going to be a very different kind of budget from the one that the same Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) introduced in 1949 to meet the political exigencies of the Liberal machine.
Before anybody pays too much attention to the views of the two hon. gentlemen I have mentioned, I should like to put alongside them the comments upon the rates of taxation in this country which have appeared in the columns of two very eminent newspapers. I mention first of all Le Devoir, which on February 18 last said this:
Les impots reglent l'activite economique d'un pays. Quand les impots deviennent excessifs. its tuent l'esprit d'initiative et le commerce aussi sure-ment que les detruit le socialisme.

The Address-Mr. Fleming
If I may attempt a free translation, Mr. Speaker, this is what I would offer:
Taxes regulate the economic activity of a country. When taxes become excessive they kill the spirit of initiative and trade as surely as socialism destroys it.
Then on the same day in the very eminent UAction Catholique the following statement appeared, and I invite my hon. and effusive friend from Montmagny-L'Islet to listen to this.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure you are strained to follow the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet in that rather nice distinction he has drawn. He says that there is a difference between overtaxation on the one hand, and bleeding the Canadian taxpayer white on the other. Well, let him have his choice. The Canadian taxpayer is being bled; his blood is running fast.
The story does not end there, Mr. Speaker. We have hon. members opposite saying in effect that the surpluses are so wonderful, and asking, Are we not glad we have them? One would have thought that it was evidence of supreme achievement when the Minister of Finance, by these extortionate rates of taxation that he has amassed with the assistance of the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet and others, has reported this evidence of gross overtaxation at the end of the year. In measuring these unparalleled blunders in national financing we will not be too ready, I am sure, to accept statements to the effect that last year's surplus was, as we were told at one stage, $356 million, at another stage some $250 million. We will rather go back and recall that before the Minister of Finance started to put $100 million in one pocket in the consolidated revenue fund, and another $100 million somewhere else, and then engage in a good deal of heavy expenditure in the closing days of the fiscal year in order to relieve himself of the embarrassment of that
huge surplus, he had about $900 million surplus which was the true measure of the government's excessive taxation last year.
It was with that alternative in mind, and other aspects of the budget that was introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) last spring, that another very eminent newspaper in this country made comment. Le Soleil, in its columns of April 12 last said this:
La presse frangaise du Quebec a accueilli avec une impression teintee de desappointement le budget de M. Abbott. Aucun journal ne lui manifeste de l'enthousiasme. La note generale est celle d'une deception.
If I may offer a free translation, Mr. Speaker, it would run like this: that the French press of Quebec greeted the budget of Mr. Abbott with a reception tinged with disappointment. No newspaper manifests any enthusiasm for it; the general note is that of a deception. Yet in the face of that very pertinent observation on this government's taxation policies we hear hon. gentlemen opposite rising now and saying with great gusto, and some evidence that they are whistling to keep up their courage, that it is impossible for the Minister of Finance to reduce taxes. Well, I think, Mr. Speaker, before we are finished with this debate ways in which the Minister of Finance could reduce taxes, if there were, on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite, any will to reduce unnecessary expenditures and to eliminate extravagance, will be fully dealt with.
But let us look now to see what the Minister of Finance himself has to say on this interesting subject. We find that he has not been silent between the sessions. He made a tour of the maritime provinces and a tour of the west. His speech of September 23 is reported thus in the Winnipeg Free Press of September 30. He says:
Taxes are high these days in Canada.
As if he had to go all the way to Winnipeg to tell the people that! And then he continues:
Are taxes too high? This, of course, is simply another way of asking. "Are we spending too much?"
I interject to say that I think there is a good deal to be said for his interpretation. He continues:
You can take my word for it that the official opposition in parliament these days seem to think that we are spending too much.
Well, I can assure the hon. gentleman that he spoke with complete accuracy when he said the official opposition in parliament these days seem to think that the government is spending too much. Nothing could be more certain.

Then he continued on his merry way. In Charlottetown on October 6 he made a speech in which he is reported to have spoken to this effect, that he would be happy if he could break even on this year's budget, but he held out the possibility of tax cuts if Canada's production keeps rising.
Mr. Speaker, we have it both ways there. The man who has delivered these excessive budgets since 1949 said he would be happy to break even on this year's federal budget; but then this member of the cabinet who will be called to the rescue of the Liberal party when he delivers his budget speech next March rose to the occasion and said that he held out the possibility of tax cuts, if Canada's production keeps rising.
Then he moved on to Vancouver. In the Vancouver Sun of October 20 the minister is reported to this effect:
Canadians may look forward to federal tax cuts but certainly not in next year's budget, finance minister Douglas Abbott said here today.
Then he is reported to have said, during the course of a 6,000-word address to the Vancouver board of trade:
To those who think the federal government will enjoy a fat surplus at the end of its fiscal year, Mr. Abbott said, "I shall be happy if we break even."
Then his interview -with the press before he made his speech is reported in this way by the Vancouver Sun:
Mr. Abbott said that this goal-
That is, the goal of improving our standard of living.
-should be reached and taxes cut-
You will note, Mr. Speaker, he is saying that taxes ought to be cut. Then he says this: -but there is little chance of its attainment by next March when the 1953 budget will be brought down.
Then he is reported in the Montreal Gazette of October 21 as having said this in his Vancouver speech:
We can confidently expect that increased production in Canada will make taxation less, despite continuing expenditures for defence and social welfare.
But Mr. Abbott added in a later interview that there is "little chance" of tax cuts in the next budget.
I am sure those words of the minister must have chilled the blood of hon. gentlemen opposite, when he intimated that there would be no tax cuts in his next budget, to be introduced next March. Because the one hope that is nourishing the political lives of hon. gentlemen opposite has been that in his 1953 budget the minister would repeat the rabbit act of 1949 when, after announcing for several previous years that taxation reductions were impossible, somehow he trotted
The Address-Mr. Fleming out substantial reductions in taxation on the eve of the election to save their political hides for the occasion.
Now at least we have the Minister of Finance saying in October that hon. gentlemen opposite, as well as the Canadian people, need not expect any taxation reductions in the next year. Well, I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite will have to do some whistling, from now on, to keep up their failing and flagging spirits.
I mentioned that the Minister of Finance had said that we of the official opposition had been saying the government is spending too much. Of course we say that. We know very well how much this government likes to spend money. This government has the idea that it helps to make votes for itself by spending money. That is one reason they are so anxious to spend so much money before the next election. How otherwise can anyone possibly attribute to sane people these reckless expenditures in which the government is indulging at the present time?
In a book I read recently I found an interesting paragraph. This is a book containing several lectures by Bertrand de Jouvenel. It is entitled "The Ethics of Redistribution", and at page 73 contains this paragraph:
The more one considers the matter, the clearer it becomes that redistribution is in effect far less a redistribution of free income from the richer to the poorer, as we imagined, than a redistribution of power from the individual to the state.
Whatever one's views may be on the observations of the author, it is clear that the spending of money on the part of a government does mean power, and the view of this government is that it does mean votes. I well recall a conversation I had with one of the ministers some six years ago, when I was commenting on wastefulness in duplicated services and expenditures on the part of the dominion and the provinces. I said to him, with regard to one expenditure in particular, "Would it not be much more sensible if the dominion and the provinces got together and shared the expenditures, so the money could be devoted to its purpose through the provinces?" With a knowing smile he said, "Oh, no; that would give"-and he mentioned by name the premier of the province in which he resided-"a chance to make votes".
Well, you see the thought of this government is that if they spend money they make votes; and that is the reason, and the only reason, you see these reckless expenditures being made at the present time. Here we have this record, one which would shock people who were not already accustomed to shocks at the hands of a spendthrift and mismanaging government.

The Address-Mr. Fleming
After having already purchased 1,153,155 neckties, the government in the first half of October spent $32,638 on more neckties. What contribution are those neckties going to make toward resisting aggression in the world? I understood that the whole basis on which the house was called upon to vote something like $2,100 million for national defence this year was that it would have the effect, first, of deterring aggression and, second, if unhappily aggression should come it would enable us to bear our fair share of the burden of resisting aggression successfully. What important functions are these neckties going to serve in resisting aggression or overcoming aggression? As the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) said in a recent radio broadcast, it may be that these neckties are to be used to bind hand and foot every aggressor who might set foot on Canadian soil.
In the eleven months up to February 29 last a total of 1,304,407 pairs of men's shoes had been purchased and orders are still being placed. We were told in a return that in the thirteen months up to April 30 last 117,800 pairs of women's shoes were purchased. I do not intend to take the time to refer again to serving forks except to comment that the scaling down of the orders for serving forks from 63,500 to 14,500 is attributable to the vigilance of the official opposition.
There are six full-time officers and 900 officers and other ranks in the reserve in the Canadian Women's Army Corps. In order to keep off the raindrops a total of
15,000	raincoats have been purchased for them.
Then there is the $839,903 which has been spent on carpets and rugs for the armed forces. As my leader pointed out, that would provide a square yard of rug or carpet for every two members of the armed forces on active service. It is quite evident that the government is showing very great concern about the purchases of rugs, carpets, neckties, raincoats and shoes.
There is no possible way of explaining or justifying expenditures on this scale except that they are being made now with a conscious view toward making friends for this government.

shortcomings in the operations of the unemployment insurance commission. I am glad the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is in the chamber because if he does not know that this sort of thing is being turned out, I think he ought to know and should have known before this. This is how it reads:
In savage tribes, where skulls are thick,
And primal passions rage,
They have a system, sure and quick,
To cure the blight of age.
For when a native's youth has fled,
And age has sapped his vim,
They simply knock him on the head,
And put an end to him.
But we in our enlightened age,
Are built of nobler stuff,
And so we look with scorn and rage,
On deeds so harsh and rough.
And when a man is old and gray,
And stooped and short of breath,
We simply take his job away,
And let him starve to death.
That was issued by the unemployment insurance commission of Canada at the expense of the taxpayers of this country. Yet the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) has the effrontery to stand before this house and say that there is no overtaxation. I tell you that there is shameful overtaxation, there is shameful extravagance in the way this government is throwing around the hard-earned money of the Canadian taxpayer.

-I should like to say something with respect to the subject of television and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a subject concerning which I hope I shall have the opportunity to say more at a later stage of the session.
If there comes about at long last the elimination of that $2.50 nuisance tax, namely the fee on radio receiving sets, the people of Canada will be able to thank the official opposition for the fight it has waged without abatement for more than a decade for the elimination of that nuisance tax.
I make this observation on television. After having taken unto itself in a most bureaucratic and paternalistic manner all control over television and in effect preventing the development of television in Canada so that this country at present, compared with the stage reached in the United Kingdom and the United States, is in a most primitive stage of development thanks to government policy and nothing else, what has been said in the throne speech by the government in offering to let private enterprise in on some of the areas which the C.B.C. is not prepared to enter is nothing but throwing to private enterprise a bone from which all meat and nourishment have been completely removed.
It is not because there has been any unwillingness or lack of enterprise in this country, apart from the government, that we have not adequate development of television in Canada. Private enterprise has been waiting for years for the government to make up its mind. Some applications for television channels have been pending before the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for more than seven years; yet the government has simply sat like a dog in a manger. It was not doing anything effective itself for the development of television and it would not let anybody else do anything. Now that they have got service established in two centres in Canada, Montreal and Toronto, and other parts of the country

are very properly complaining about the concentration of government service in these two areas while the rest of the country is helping develop in areas where there is no possible opportunity of competition for the C.B.C. It is in keeping with the bureaucratic attitude of this government that they foster monopoly. I am sure you well remember, Mr. Speaker, when you and I were members of the special committee on radio broadcasting in 1946 that in reply to a question I put to him, the chairman of the board of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation said he thought that competition from the large privately owned radio stations had been a good thing for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation because it helped to keep the C.B.C. on their toes. Well, Mr. Speaker, if that was true with regard to radio broadcasting in 1946, why not allow a little competition with respect to television in this year 1952?
Here is private capital and private enterprise willing to take all the risks involved if this bureaucratic government, with its mania for monopoly and bureaucracy, will not restrain the development of something for which the people of Canada are crying. Last December the number of television receiving sets in this country was estimated at 60,000. I am prepared to assume that by this time it must be 100,000. Canada has engineers and technicians and artists who are capable of helping this country lead in the development of television. The reason Canada is not leading the field is that this government is stifling and thwarting this development.

I rise to support the amendment of my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), calling as it does upon this government to introduce at this session legislation to establish a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial participation. I may tell you, sir, that there will be several other members of this group who will speak in this debate and join in urging the government to give serious consideration to what is set forth in our amendment.
The reason we shall repeatedly return to the attack, so far as the need for health insurance is concerned, is that it is becoming quite apparent that the government of the day does not realize how important this question is to the people of Canada. The record, so far as the Liberal party is concerned, supports the statement I have just
The Address-Mr. Knowles made, namely that the government does not recognize the importance of this question. How could any Liberal claim to recognize its importance in view of the fact that it has been in the platform of the Liberal party ever since 1919. Despite the fact it has been in the platform of that party for all those years, when I drew that to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) last June his reply was, yes, it is in our platform and it has been there for 33 years, but surely you do not expect us to bring it in overnight.
I remind you, sir, that on top of all the committee reports and investigations that have been made, evidence of which was placed before this house again yesterday by my colleague the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), a year ago last June we had what we thought was a promise that there would be a special committee on health insurance during the session which met in the early part of 1952. We did not feel that another committee was necessary in view of all the inquiries that had been conducted. But despite our feeling that a committee was not necessary, we were glad to know that we were making at least that much progress. We dared to hope that the promised committee would be set up, and that it would have a result comparable to the result which followed the 1950 committee on old age security, namely that there would be legislation in this important field.
Despite what we thought was a clear-cut promise that there would be such a committee at the first session of 1952, when we met and asked when that committee was to be set up we were informed that the government had decided not to establish such a committee at that session. We are now in another session-indeed this is the third session since the one in 1951 when the promise to take at least the action of setting up a committee was suggested-and still we have no suggestion of any action by this government on the question of health insurance. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the record is a clear indication of the failure of the government and its supporters to realize how important this question is to the Canadian people.
I regret that the other two opposition parties in this house, in my view, despite their professed support of the principle of health insurance, are playing into the government's hands. The Progressive Conservatives, in their amendment, have asked for another inquiry into this question. If anything could be more unnecessary I do not know wbat it is. The information and material on the

The Address-Mr. Knowles basis of which legislation could be enacted is already abundant and complete. Our friends to the left in the Social Credit group profess support of a program of health insurance, but the other night in speaking about this matter the leader of the- party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), suggested that what was needed in relation to this question was to move gradually. They may mean by that the support which the member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) suggested today, but I suggest that to tell this government to set up another inquiry, as the Tories are doing, or to suggest to the members of the government that they move gradually, as the Social Crediters are doing, is to play right into the hands of the Liberals who are quite prepared to stall on this question as they have done already for 33 years.
We feel we are expressing the views of the Canadian people when we say that this is one of the important questions that should be dealt with at this session. It is not one of those questions that should be bandied about during the course of an election campaign, with the promise to set up a committee in the next parliament and perhaps take action in the parliament following that one. This is a question that calls for action at this session of parliament.
I have been referring, Mr. Speaker, to the importance of this question. We do wish we could impress upon the government what it means to the average Canadian citizen not to be able to afford the full measure of health services and health protection that modern medical science is in a position to offer, if we could only organize the financing of the cost of medical services.
According to the 1951 census figures, some of which are now coming to us, in Canada's twenty largest cities we find 27-8 per cent of the total population, In those twenty largest cities 49-8 per cent of all wage and salary earners received an annual income of less than $2,000. According to another survey made by the dominion bureau of statistics in 1947-48, it was ascertained that families in that year-I admit I am speaking about different years but one has to take these figures as he gets them and allow for any adjustments that should be made-who had incomes of $2,000 or less were able to spend on health care not more than $70 in any case. The figure ranged from $70 per year down for all those with incomes of $2,000 per year or less.
Other figures which I have obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics show that in 1950, which was in between the two years I have already mentioned-, the average stay in hospital in Canada was 10-5 days, at an average cost per patient day of $8.13 or


an average total hospital expense of $85.36. That is the average annual hospital bill, $85.36. Yet the survey of family income and expenditure to which I have already referred indicated that the people with incomes of $2,000 or less were able to spend on all health care, in the course of a year, only $70 or less.
I could go on and show likewise, from figures for the year 1951, that the total expenditure on health in Canada in that year made by Canadians privately was $496 million, which results in an average family expenditure of $129.50. What I ask hon. members to note is this. If the average hospital cost is $85.36 and the average total family expenditure on health per year is $129.50, what is the position of the large number of wage and salary earners who, according to the other survey to which I referred, are able to spend only $70 a year or less on all health, medical and hospital care?
