I think not. But even if my hon. friend wants to contend for purposes of his position, whatever it is, that there are some families in which there is more than one earner, I ask him to consider the families where there is only one earner, and that is the case in most of them. They are able to spend on all health, hospital and medical care only $70 a year or less, whereas the annual average cost for hospital care is $85.36 per family, and the average per family for medical expenses is $129.50. It simply means that there is a whole section of our population which is getting-because it cannot afford to pay for it-less of health, hospital and medical care than, on an average,

would seem to be the minimum requirement for Canadians at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, when you interpret that situation in terms of ill health, suffering, mental anguish and concern over unpaid hospital and doctors' bills, I suggest that we in Canada are submitting ourselves to a social, psychological and economic loss that common sense would dictate we should not endure.
In the course of this debate I have heard a number of hon. members comment on the large number of people who receive help from doctors despite the fact that they cannot afford to pay for it. I have heard references to many cases where doctors receive far less than would be their normal fee for the type of service they are giving, and I recognize all of that to be true. But what I ask hon. members to bear in mind is that many Canadians need medical care, the attention of doctors and hospitalization, but because they cannot afford it they do not seek it or do not ask for it, or in cases of necessity they put it off for much longer than, for the sake of their health, should be the case. What we are suggesting is that we should have a plan that is based on common sense, on organization, on pooling and sharing this problem so that all our people can get the best of medical and hospital care that is available.
This idea is not one that we alone advocate. It has been put forward, as I say, by the Liberals ever since their convention in 1919, and the library shelves contain books and periodicals which are full of arguments in support of the whole principle of health insurance. In its green book proposals to the provinces in 1945 the dominion government spelled it out very well when it said:
Health insurance enables the cost of illness to be prepaid, so that by paying regular sums when they are well people are able to meet the costs of illness when they are ill without being financially crippled.
The government also said at that time:
Health insurance not only enables individuals to prepay their medical costs, but does this in such a way as to secure a wide pooling of risks and distribution of costs in much the same manner as any other form of insurance.
I also hold in my hand an extremely interesting little booklet put out during the war by the wartime information board, mainly for the benefit of the armed forces. It is entitled "Canadian Affairs", volume I, No. 21, November 15, 1944. Its subject was "Canada Plans Security". It was written by a gentleman who was then not a civil servant but who is now one of the top and most esteemed civil servants in this country, namely Dr. George F. Davidson, deputy minister of welfare in
The Address-Mr. Knowles the Department of National Health and Welfare. In this pamphlet, Dr. Davidson says:
There are still gaps in our social security program. Chief among these concerns the question of illness. When sickness strikes, it strikes with a two-edged sword. Not only does the workman lose his pay during the period he is away from work- worse than that, he has to bear the crushing blow of medical, hospital, and other expenses, running sometimes into hundreds of dollars.
He then goes on to say that health insurance is the remedy. Then he develops certain details, gives us the history of the study that has been given to health insurance, and reminds us of the proposals that have been made. Then toward the end of the pamphlet, having summed up various aspects of social security, including a health insurance program, which he felt were in the cards so far as the future was concerned, this is what he said under the heading of "What It All Costs":
But not all of this represents additional cost. We are meeting now from our own individual resources, as best we can, the heavy medical and hospital expenses that we encounter from time to time. We are carrying now in large part the cost of our own unemployment, eating up our savings when we fall out of work. We are paying now, to whatever extent we can, through private insurance plans and through savings of one kind or another, for the possibility of retirement or death.
So, in large part, government intervention to provide these social schemes would mean we would pay by taxes and contributions for what we have been trying-unsuccessfully on the whole-to purchase privately.
The concluding paragraph of this extremely interesting pamphlet commences with these very telling words:
Canada, in short, can afford to provide security for her people. She cannot afford not to provide it.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, when the special committee on old age security met in 1950, it found it impossible not to deal to some extent with the question of health insurance, for it as well as other matters was related to the whole question of old age security. Despite the fact that this matter was outside of our terms of reference, our report which was tabled in the House of Commons on June 28, 1950 dealt-briefly, it is true but nevertheless it dealt with it-with the question of health insurance; and this is what it said in part:
It has been estimated, however, that the over-all cost of a comprehensive system of health insurance would probably be not less than $300 million annually, although it must be added that a large proportion of such an amount would represent not a new burden on the people of Canada, but merely a rechannelling of existing expenditures on various forms of health care.
That in the main, Mr. Speaker, is what we are advocating when we put forward the claim for a program of health insurance. It is not in the main something new so far as health services are concerned, although it is true



The Address-Mr. Knowles that a great extension is needed. What we are asking is that there be a rechannelling of our expenditures, a pooling of the burden of health costs so that on a common-sense basis all our Canadian people can get the care they need and that medical science and our medical people are able in this modern age to provide.
It has already been indicated-indeed it was by the hon. member for York South yesterday-what illness means in terms of lost man hours at work. The elimination of that economic loss would have to be set off against any additional cost that health insurance might involve. And I suggest that as a modern civilization that knows how to span the world, as we do, by amazing means of transportation and communication, we are just being stupid if we do not organize the financing of our health services so that all our Canadian people can have the benefit of the best health services that are available today. I hope that the other members on the opposition side of the house will join with us as this session proceeds in pressing upon the government the urgency of this matter.
It is not something to be the subject of a further inquiry, as the official opposition suggests. It is not something to be approached gradually, as the leader of the Social Credit party suggests. It has been going on gradually for a third of a century or more. It is something that is of concern to Canadians now;, it is something that calls for legislation at this particular session. While we wait for these further inquiries that the Tories here suggest; while we move gradually as the Social Credit leader would suggest, people are being sick and are not getting the attention they need; people are dying unnecessarily; people are burdened with the costs of medical and hospital bills that are around their necks as long as they live. And not only that; Canada as a whole suffers a great loss because we do not make it possible for all that medical science knows to be brought to bear upon the life and the health of our Canadian people.
I hope that with greater urgency being pressed upon the government by the entire opposition, the government will realize that this is not a question on which they can play politics any longer, that they can put off until after the next election. It is a question for action at this session of parliament; and if the members of the cabinet are not prepared, on their own initiative, to do something about it, I hope the private members on the Liberal side of the house, in their caucuses behind closed doors, will press upon

the government that this is one subject about which they must do something at this session of parliament.
I wish to say a few words about another question that comes under the heading of social security, namely old age security. It seems to be a matter of pride on the part of supporters of the Liberal government that at long last they responded to our demands and the pressure of public opinion in this country for the removal of the means test from the old age pension-and it was a splendid move. But those same Liberals seem to be quite satisfied with the fact that the pension being paid to our citizens 70 years of age and over is only $40 a month. Surely, Mr. Speaker, it does not need to be argued at all that that amount is hopelessly and woefully inadequate, and that if we do accept the principles of social security that were outlined in this booklet by Dr. Davidson from which I quoted a few moments ago, the time has come to increase the amount of the old age security payment to a figure more commensurate with today's cost of living. I would suggest in responsible terms that it should be not less than $60 a month. There are many who feel -and personally I share that feeling-that the amount should be even higher than that.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that with the tendency in industry generally to retire people at the age of 65, we are being most unfair to our people to leave that gap between 65 and 70 with the means test. Thus another change that should be made is that the means test should be taken off at age 65.
Similarly, Mr. Speaker, I feel-and I was glad to note one of the new Liberal members of the house the other day expressing this view as well-the time has come to remove completely the means test from the pension _ paid to our blind citizens. Surely with that special handicap which these people have we should do our best to make up for it slightly by giving them a pension not on the basis of means but as a matter of right as some compensation which their fellow Canadians feel they should have.
It is perfectly proper for anyone who listens to what I am saying, calling as I am for extensions in the field of social security- health and old age security, removal of the means test for the blind, and so on-to raise questions about the cost. And that of course is a very popular reply on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and on the part of government supporters; that it is all very well provided that we are prepared to pay for it. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when we are considering this whole question of the cost of social security benefits what we

The Address-Mr. Knowles
should do is look at them in a proper perspective. We should relate them to the total productive capacity of the country. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), and others on the government side like to create the impression that a disproportionately large amount of our national income is going into social security. We are told that in round figures our budget is something over $4 billion. We are told that a little over half that, $2 billion, is for national defence, and that nearly half of the other half, or nearly one-quarter of the total of our national budget, is going into social security.
There came to my desk a few days ago, as no doubt there came to the desks of all hon. members, a further document from the research division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. This one is social security series memorandum No. 14. I congratulate this department on the tremendous amount of very valuable research they have done in all aspects of social security. But this one seems to be designed to support the contention of government supporters that too large a proportion of our money is going into social security or at least as much as the country can stand. For example, to take the extreme case that is built up in this memorandum, I find that on page 15 reference is made to the fiscal year ended March 31, 1951, and to the total expenditures of the federal government, of all provincial governments and of all municipalities, and then they are added up. As against that total there is set the total amount spent at each of these levels in health and social welfare expenditures, and they are added up, and then the one total is set against the other in terms of a percentage. On that basis we are told that for the fiscal year that ended March 31, 1951, the total amount of health and social welfare expenditures was $1,058,738,000. This was out of total expenditures by all levels of government of $4,858,305,000. In other words the argument, or the case, is set before us in these terms: 21-8 per cent of the total of the revenues of all governments was spent on health and social welfare expenditures.
Before I make the main comment I want to make on that -I should like to point out that included in these health and social welfare expenditures are not only all expenditures that could be considered as such by the provincial and municipal governments, but in the case of the federal government there are included old age pensions, pensions for the blind, family allowances, unemployment insurance benefits, veterans' pensions, war veterans' allowances, hospital and other allowances for veterans, and even prairie
farm emergency fund payments. Thus one must not think that that figure I have given of over a billion dollars relates to the more exclusive forms of social security as we usually understand them.
I shall come back to that in a moment. But even before I do, what it seems to me this house should realize is that while this total sum, this large sum of $1,058,738,000 that the department was able to build up, is 21-8 per cent of the revenues of the three levels of government, it is only 4-9 per cent of the gross national product for the year for which these figures were prepared.
I believe a society such as ours that believes in social security, that believes in bearing one another's burdens, that believes in the whole idea of community responsibility and of being civilized, is not going too far and indeed, is not going far enough when it devotes-even at the highest figure, the department can build up-only 4-9 per cent of its gross national product on these various health and welfare expenditures.
Those are the figures, of course, for the year ended March 31, 1951. We are now in a different year, and in the meantime we have had a change in the old age program. Hence those figures will be different when they come out for another year. But I am satisfied that the increase in the amount spent on these various items will not represent any higher percentage of the gross national product because the gross national product is going up. The figure for that earlier year was $21,241 million. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has estimated that for this fiscal year it will be $22,500 million; so the percentage will probably be no greater when we have the comparable report for the current fiscal year.
But with respect to the current fiscal year the estimates indicate that we have voted $322 million for old age security. That is one of the figures ministers use to build up the large sum they say we are spending on social security, and they give it to us in terms of its percentage of the national revenue. But I submit that a realistic perspective is to look at it in terms of the gross national product, of the total wealth we are producing in this country.
The Minister of Finance says that this year our gross national product will be $22,500 million. Well, the $322 million which we allocate for old age security is only 1 [DOT] 4 per cent of that gross national product. And yet our senior citizens, 70 years of age and over, number about 5 per cent of the population. That, in straightforward and realistic terms, is what we are doing. We are allocating 1-4 per cent of the gross national product to 5

The Address-Mr. Knowles per cent of the citizens of this country. If there were acceptance of my suggestion that it should be increased to not less than $60 per month, the percentage would be increased only 2-1 per cent of the gross national product for 5 per cent of the population of the country. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, therefore, that a suggestion of that kind is not at all out of line. It is not as far as our older citizens might ask us to go; surely we should not fail to go at least that far.
Similarly, if one built up the other items for which I have argued-the removal of the means test after the age of 65, the removal of the means test so far as blind pensioners are concerned, a health insurance program, and so on-all these put together would still leave the total amount we would spend on health and social welfare at a figure not much over five or six per cent of the gross national product or of the total wealth we produce in this country.
I suggest that if we were to spend that amount of money, particularly that portion of it which would be in a health insurance program, the saving in the loss of man-days of work and the general improvement that we would create in the lives of our people could result in a comparable increase in the gross national product. I say that what we are proposing is not that some Santa Claus should hand things out; rather, what we are proposing is just plain, ordinary common sense, and I am satisfied that is the way the people of this country feel.
I hope the proposals we are making will be considered by the government in that light, that it will realize we are not asking that the Canadian people be given something for nothing, but rather that we are simply asking that the people of the country who produce the nation's wealth, who are responsible for our huge gross national product, get back a reasonable share of that gross national product, and that they get part of that reasonable proportion or share in the form of social security and in the form of protection of their health so they can enjoy life as it should be possible in Canada at this time.
Before my time comes to a close may I touch briefly on two or three other subjects. I join wholeheartedly with those who have called upon the government to take action at this session in connection with the means test as it applies to the War Veterans Allowance Act. Hon. members know that last session, when the act was amended, some of us were not at all satisfied with the income ceilings that were retained in the act, which permit in most cases only $10 a month of other income to a burnt-out pensioner, be he single or married.
[Mr. Knowles.j

It is not without significance that the Canadian Legion so soon after that legislation was passed has again launched a campaign, which I support, calling for an increase in the permissible income ceiling. Everyone knows how responsible that body is, and I suggest real attention should be paid by the government to the fact that they are back already insisting that something be done about the means test under the War Veterans Allowance Act. For my part, I think the allowance should have been $60 and $120 for single and married persons respectively, as the Legion asked. But at least action should be taken at this session to raise substantially the permissible income ceiling provided in the act.
Similarly I still feel, and hon. members have heard me mention this repeatedly on the floor of the house, that something should be done for our retired civil servants, particularly those in the lower income brackets. During the years I have been urging the government to take action on this matter, other governments have taken action. In the United States they have passed a special provision for increasing on a percentage basis, within certain brackets, the pensions of those already retired. Recently there has been a second pensions increase bill in the United Kingdom, raising the pensions of those already retired. There has been recognition by those governments that while those people were retired on the pension rates provided by the law at the time they retired, conditions over which the pensioners had no control have increased their cost of living, and that they are entitled to a better break.
I hope our Canadian retired civil servants will be given consideration at this session. I could hope that the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) was not off the beam yesterday, as I fear he was, when he expressed the view that in the speech from the throne he saw that something was going to be done for them. I am afraid the hon. member had not read it carefully, because the speech from the throne says only that the Civil Service Superannuation Act is to be amended. That affects only those who are still in the service. I contend that something must also be done for those already retired, particularly those in the lower brackets.
Before this session gets along much farther there will be opportunity for some of us to call to the attention of the government other items of unfinished business left over from former sessions. There will be the question of the check-off of trade union dues, which I hope the government will endorse this year. There is also the question to which the Prime

Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made reference the other night, namely the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes. I would remind hon. members what happened at the last session. My motion seeking removal of the 4 per cent limitation passed the house unanimously, but the Minister of Finance chose not to change the act accordingly. The people of Canada expect a better deal than that this time. My motion is on the order paper again this session, and I hope greater consideration will be given to what I am satisfied are the wishes of the Canadian people in respect of this matter of medical expenses in relation to income tax.
One other thought, and I shall take my seat-and I believe I shall have finished within my 40 minutes-and that is to express the hope that there will not be a delay of ten years, or even nine years or five years, in dealing with the question as to how future redistributions of seats in the House of Commons are to be effected. It is not my purpose at this moment nor is there time to revive the feeling which existed in the house last June because of the redistribution which was effected at that time. The feelings which some of us had have been confirmed by the feelings we found to exist in our constituencies and in various parts of Canada during the recess.
The point I wish to make is that there was a much wider feeling this year than ever before that the time has come for redistribution to be carried out by an independent commission. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) suggested on several occasions that the time to raise the question of an independent commission-although I did not agree with him-was not when we were dealing with redistribution. He suggested that he would be glad to have me join with him at the first session after that last redistribution in proposing that this matter of finding another way to do it should be given serious study. I hope when the hon. member for Quebec South gets back to the house he will remember the suggestion he made and will call upon the government to set up a committee at this session of parliament to study the whole question of having future redistributions of the seats in this House of Commons effected by an independent commission.
There is a good deal of dissatisfaction in the country with what was done last June and July. That dissatisfaction is very evident in my own province where the new constituencies vary all the way from one with only
40,000	population to one with over 81,000.
The Address-Mr. Dickey No one can possibly defend such a discrepancy. The only answer to that kind of situation and the kind of boundary lines that are drawn by parliamentary committees is to get this business out of parliament and have it done by an independent commission so the people of Canada will feel that the job is being done for them and not for hon. members who happen to be sitting in parliament at the time the matter is under review.
I hope this matter will receive consideration along with the others that I have suggested. And once again I press upon the government as a matter of top importance at this session the urgent need for a nation-wide program of health insurance as is proposed in the C.C.F. amendment now before this house.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. Dickey (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words are of sincere congratulation to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. These two new members have covered themselves and their constituents with glory by their maiden speeches, and I am sure all hon. members look forward to their continued participation in the debates of this house.
I want to express my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney). These two gentlemen have been well and favourably known in this house for many years, and we wish them every success in carrying out the new and heavy responsibilities which have fallen upon them.
It is a pleasure to me to speak this afternoon for the first time through the fine voiceraising equipment which has been installed in this chamber by a firm located in the constituency of Halifax. As this system continues to be in operation I hope that not only hon. members of the house but members of the public who' come into the galleries to follow our deliberations will find it of great benefit in properly following the proceedings.
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) dealt in some detail with complaints which he had received regarding two construction projects which are under way in his province for the Department of National Defence. No one is more anxious to receive notice of complaints of this nature than the ministers of the departments of this government who are responsible for construction activities of this kind. From time to time we do get word of complaints, and those complaints are quickly and thoroughly investigated. I am happy to say that on almost every occasion careful investigation
124	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Dickey satisfies the concern of those who have brought the matter to the attention of the proper authority.
I assure the hon. member that so far as the Department of Defence Production and Defence Construction Limited are concerned, we believe that conditions at both the locations mentioned are satisfactory. However, immediate inquiry will be made to establish that fact. We will welcome and will co-operate fully in any investigation conducted by the committee on defence expenditures when that committee is set up.
I should like to deal briefly with certain suggestions which have been made outside this house that the morale of Canada's armed forces serving in Europe as part of our NATO army and air force leaves something to be desired. I had the privilege and I may say the pleasure of visiting our army and air force units in Europe and the United Kingdom some three weeks ago. From my observations and experience I think I can assure the house and the country that there is definitely no serious difficulty. The morale of our forces is extremely high and satisfactory.
Perhaps if I gave a brief resume of what I saw in Europe you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members would be in a better position to judge the facts. The main burden of the complaints which I have heard is in connection with our army component of the NATO forces, which consists of the 27th brigade stationed in and around Hanover in Western Germany. Hanover is a large city situated approximately 45 miles west of the boundary of the east zone of Germany, and is therefore quite close to the iron curtain. It was quite an experience to a person like myself to feel that I was so near to the border of that area of the world which is causing us so much concern at the present time.
For the past few years Hanover has been the centre of a large concentration of displaced persons, and it is only recently that the city has got back to a more normal and ordinary life. It would require some time for me to describe the various units of the brigade and the exact nature of the quarters in which they are located. Suffice it to say that the Canadian troops are all quartered in excellent permanent barracks with living quarters for officers, N.C.O.'s and men that are the equal of anything in this country and in my experience distinctly better than most. Adequate canteen and recreational facilities are available to our troops in the form of movie theatres, canteens, reading rooms and the like. There are in our barrack areas gymnasiums and one excellent indoor


swimming pool which provide facilities for indoor exercise both as a matter of drill and also free time relaxation. A program of rigorous training and a sports program give more than adequate opportunity for outdoor exercise to all our troops. The sports program includes everything from boxing and gymnastics to cross-country running.
The medical, dental and postal services are excellent. Our field ambulance unit has a small hospital for the immediate use of the Canadian troops, and a large and well-equipped British military hospital is available for more serious cases.
I was particularly impressed with the nature and extent of the educational program available to our brigade troops. I formed the opinion that it is by all standards a better and wider program than is available at the present time to similar troops in Canada. It is true that the opportunities for giving time for an educational program are better in the conditions under which the brigade finds itself in Germany, and there has perhaps been more incentive to the personnel to take advantage of the educational facilities that are available. However, the fact is that they are entering into the educational program very well indeed.
One of the main matters of concern to any troops or any army is that of food. The ration situation of our brigade and all our NATO forces is extremely good indeed. We are drawing rations from the United States quartermaster's corps supplemented to Canadian scale, and there is absolutely no complaint with the food at all. The personnel of the brigade are as you would expect. The officers are largely young men, almost 100 per cent of them having overseas service during world war II. The same is true of the N.C.O.'s and men. They are all first-class young Canadians, and from my observation I would say they are enjoying their military service as much as any Canadians could be expected to enjoy being outside of Canada for the length of time and under the conditions under which they are serving.
The general impression the brigade gives to any visitor, and certainly which it gave to me, is one of smartness and efficiency. I was able to make inquiries outside of the brigade in the Hanover area and also in other parts of Germany and in England. I was informed by people who know that the Canadian brigade gave a superb performance in recent extensive manoeuvres in West Germany, and I know that they gave a very fine account of themselves.
What about morale? As you, Mr. Speaker, and many members of the house are aware,

morale is an indefinable thing. It is a composite of pride of service, pride in your formation and pride in your unit, of confidence in the leadership that the officers and N.C.O.'s give to the men. It is a composite of general satisfaction with food and living conditions and a realization that reasonable facilities for recreation, sports and amusements are available.
All these elements exist so far as our brigade is concerned, and I can assure hon. members that the result is that the morale of the brigade is very high indeed. Reports indicating that there is some concern about low morale have arisen, I understand, from newspaper stories dealing with the subject which were based not on personal evidence but on secondhand opinions and suggestions. Having been on the spot, I can say most sincerely that these suggestions are not soundly based.
I was interested after returning from Europe when several statements by other people who had had an experience similar to mine were brought to my attention. For example, in the Hamilton Spectator of November 15 there is an account given by a resident of Dundas. It reads as follows:
. . . though he was no authority on military procedure, he and his companion, having spent twelve days in Germany and considerable time at Hanover where the 27th brigade is stationed, were of the opinion that the morale of the troops was fine. Their main complaint to Mr. Bowen and himself, he said, was that they did not have enough to keep them busy.
I am sure the reference to their not having enough to keep them busy did not arise from statements by the troops that they did not find their training sufficiently active and rigorous, because the training program is exceptionally good. However, young Canadians in a foreign land do like to get around and see the country in which they are living, and many of our troops find that their inability to speak German limits their activities in this direction. In the Montreal Gazette of November 17 there is a story from Ottawa reporting statements made by Brigadier W. C. Coke, now retiring from the army as director general of medical services. The article reads:
"I have just returned from Germany after visiting every unit of the brigade", Brigadier Coke said.
That is the 27th brigade.
"I found nothing wrong with morale or welfare." He added that on a recent exercise "Very senior British officers expressed admiration of the bearing and fitness of this formation. This brigade is rated second to none in Germany. I have never seen a brigade training under peacetime conditions exhibit a higher degree of esprit de corps."
I can confirm every word of that statement by Brigadier Coke, and my considered
The Address-Mr. Dickey opinion is that the morale of the 27th brigade is extremely good indeed.
The other components of our NATO forces are two fighter wings of the R.C.A.F. There has been no real suggestion that these units are not satisfactory from the point of view of morale and everything else so far as I know, but having visited them I think I should say that they present a most satisfactory picture to anyone coming to see how they are getting along. As you know, Mr. Speaker, we are up to date on our commitments to our NATO allies. The fact is that the six F-86 squadrons that we have in Europe form the largest number of fighters considered fully capable of dealing with the Russian MIG-15. Those Canadian planes, which have been proven in combat in Korea, are now stationed one wing in France and one wing in England. They have proven themselves to be ready to meet whatever may be before them.
The first Canadian fighter wing is at North Luffenham. They are established there in permanent R.A.F. barracks at a very fine R.A.F. airdrome. It could be nothing but a pleasure for anyone to see how well they are getting along, and the excellent facilities they have. The three squadrons are all happy and indulging in very detailed and busy competition among themselves on matters of fitness. The pilots are obviously delighted with their aircraft. Their pride is helped by the fact that they realize that their colleagues in all the other air forces on the continent are jealous of the fine planes and are looking forward to having comparable equipment themselves.
One fighter squadron at North Luffenham reached that base by means of operation "Leapfrog I", in which those planes were flown from Canada to England. The second Canadian fighter wing is stationed at a new airfield which has been built for the NATO forces in France. The planes arrived there as a result of operation Leapfrog II, in which they were all flown from Canada direct to their airfield in France. This was one of the finest operations that has been carried out by any air force since the end of world war II. The arrival of this squadron in France under these conditions made a tremendous impression on all the members of the NATO alliance in Europe. The airport itself is still partially under construction, that is to say the runways are complete and the marguerites, but some of the living accommodation and other facilities were not completed at the time the airfield was occupied. The construction is going ahead satisfactorily, and while personnel met very severe weather conditions during the period in which they did

The Address-Mr. Dickey not have full occupancy of their living quarters, they put up with this discomfort in good spirit. I am sure they all look back with satisfaction on the way No. 2 fighter wing occupied that airfield and brought it to fighting efficiency under very difficult circumstances.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, may I say that neither the 27th brigade nor the R.C.A.F. units in our NATO forces have any peers in Europe today, and we can all be extremely proud of the manner in which they have conducted themselves.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with another question which has many aspects, one of which is closely connected with the question of morale in all our armed forces, whether at home or abroad. This is the very generalized and repetitious criticisms about procurement for the armed forces which we have been hearing over the last few months. This criticism is always accompanied by general remarks regarding waste, extravagance and unnecessary expenditures. I think it is not unfair to say that these criticisms, are founded on the allegation that the items that have been singled out for attention are examples of expenditures which are unjustified, either in their nature or in their extent.
A good example of this type of criticism can be found in the remarks made by the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) during this debate last evening. As an introduction to what I have to say on the question -my remarks will not be directed solely to the hon. member's statement but to similar statements made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) this afternoon-I should like to quote what the hon. member for Middlesex East said at page 89 of Hansard for November 25:
We see where the Department of Defence Production has purchased within the past year almost one million dollars worth of broadloom rugs. People do not mind paying for airplanes, guns and other supplies for our troops, but I think the people of Canada are getting sick and tired of this arm chair army for which we are buying supplies.
I regard that as a very significant and illuminating statement, Mr. Speaker. I should like to examine it in some detail, as it emphasizes the kind of thinking that is going on in the ranks of the official opposition and the manner in which they are employing half truths in order to make some baseless suggestions and to pattern innuendoes in an attempt to create an atmosphere of suspicion and bad feeling. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), who spoke earlier this afternoon, dealt with this kind of thing very briefly but quite effectively when he pointed
TMr. Dickey.]
out the work that had been done last year by the defence expenditures committee in examining and putting on the record the facts in relation to these matters which have been raised. It is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that we have heard of the rugs, the boots and other matters that have been mentioned.
The purpose, I presume, of these baseless suggestions is to achieve some political damage in so far as this government is concerned. I am afraid they will achieve some very different purpose which I shall suggest in a moment. First of all I should like to draw attention to the facts relating to the purchase of rugs, to see just exactly what they are.
The statement is:
' We see where the Department of Defence Production has purchased within the past year almost one million dollars worth of broadloom rugs.
This is the fact. The purchases of broadloom rugs from April 1950 to date are approximately $1 million. But the way in which the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) spoke, as well as other members of the official opposition who have been dealing with these problems, leaves the impression that this bald statement of an expenditure of $1 million for a certain purpose is all the information that is available.
I should like to bring to the attention of the hon. member for Middlesex East, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) the proceedings of a committee of parliament which sat last session and on which certain members of the official opposition were extremely active members. The proceedings of that committee have been published. I hold in my hand a copy of the proceedings, No. 15, which deals with the evidence that was given on Tuesday, June 10, 1952, and it has been available to the hon. member for Middlesex East and to all the other members of this house-and for that matter to the members of the public-since some time toward the end of June of last year. The question of rugs, which was dealt with in some twenty words by the hon. member for Middlesex East, was dealt with in that committee in its proceedings of that particular day as follows. This is a statement made by the deputy minister of national defence, who was dealing seriously with this particular problem. I may say that I am sorry to put this long quotation on Hansard, Mr. Speaker, but I think it should be done. This is what he said:
The next item is rugs and carpets. Rugs and carpets are slightly more complicated a category to explain in that there are quite a few articles under the heading of rugs and carpets. Included in these are not only the type of rug of a size 9 feet by 12

feet which is placed on the floor of lounges and messes but the kind of matting used on the interior decks of a number of ships.
I might perhaps try to outline to the members of the committee what the various rugs are used for. A rug or carpet 6 feet 9 inches by 9 feet is provided in each officer's single quarter. A small rug 2 feet 3 inches by 4 feet 6 inches is provided as something to cover the concrete or linoleum floor alongside the bed of each man in the other ranks single quarters. In lounges, officers lounges and NCO's lounges and men's lounges in the active force, larger rugs 9 feet by 12 feet are provided on the general basis of one per 200 square feet of floor area. The allowance for the reserve force is just one half of that-one per 400 feet of floor area.
In hospitals there is provided in sunrooms or solaria one per 300 square feet of floor area and, in addition, there are a limited number provided at government expense in married quarters at isolated units. We have found by experience that it is more economical to furnish completely a married quarter at an isolated station-and by isolated I mean really isolated such as Aklavik, Goose Bay, some of the stations on the northwest highway system, and so on-than it is to move the furnishings of the dependents. There is quite a substantial saving on the transportation charges and the cost of furnishing isolated married quarters completely is less than paying those transportation charges.
That is the basis then of the issue of the various rugs. Now, the number required in this two-year period would necessarily be quite large by reason of the substantial construction program that is now being carried on. All new single quarters for men are provided with one of these small throw rugs I mention as are all new NCO's quarters. The numbers which have been ordered are related not only to what was being constructed during the period in question but also to the quarters scheduled to come to completion during the subsequent twelvemonth period.
That is a much different thing than a bald statement that we have spent $1 million on broadloom rugs.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is the statement which I will repeat again from Hansard:
... but I think the people of Canada are getting sick and tired of this arm chair army for which we are buying supplies.
I am not going to make any comment on the appropriateness of applying to the general buying of these supplies the suggestion that they are being bought for an arm chair army; but I would ask the hon. member if it is buying rugs for an arm chair army to buy rugs to go in sunrooms and solaria of military hospitals; if it is buying rugs for an arm chair army to provide, on a logical basis, rugs for married quarters at Aklavik, Goose Bay and stations on the northwest highway system; if it is buying rugs for an arm chair army to provide one small rug in the quarters of airmen, sailors and soldiers under training in various parts of this country-in air stations all over western Canada, in naval stations on both coasts far from their homes; if it is buying rugs for an arm chair army to provide one small rug to put in the rooms occupied by those young men. If that is buying rugs or anything else for an arm chair army, then
The Address-Mr. Dickey my understanding of any term of that kind is much different from the understanding of the hon. member.
This, Mr. Speaker, I think is true of much of the criticism that we have been hearing both last session and this one. We are hearing repeated this afternoon by the hon. member for Eglinton the same bald statements which were made the last session and which were thoroughly dealt with in the committee on defence expenditures. The hon. member for Eglinton mentioned boots. In this particular issue of the proceedings of the defence expenditures committee there are three pages of evidence given by the deputy minister of national defence dealing with boots alone, in which he went into detail as to the numbers of the armed forces that had to be supplied with boots, the scales of issue and the calculation of the supplies necessary for stockpiling for possible mobilization, with the single exception that the actual numbers of mobilization stores would not be given. I think the house will agree that it would be extremely unwise for us to give an indication of that kind, as to what our mobilization plans might be. But these statements and criticisms are repeated, not in the light of the information that is available to the members who are speaking as well as to every other member of the house and to the public, but as if what they say-the bald figure-is the only information that is available. Mr. Speaker, I submit that that procedure is dealing with these things in the way of putting before this house and the country as half truths matters that are not only capable of explanation but which have already been explained.
My original point was that this matter had a close connection with the morale of our forces. It has a connection in this sense. The suggestion is made that these supplies are being purchased in an extravagant and unreasonable manner in order to give us supplies of rugs which are not used or to which the people to whom they are issued for use are not entitled, or that there is some other strange reason for procuring these things. The officers of the Department of National Defence-as I am sure it is obvious from the material that was supplied by that department to the defence expenditures committee- have gone to the greatest lengths they can go to explain why these things are required. Yet after the committee has sat, and after the proceedings are published and available for the use of anybody who wishes to use them, the same baseless arguments are put forward and the same senseless suggestions are made that there is waste and extravagance which has not been explained.

The Address-Mr. Dickey Mistakes have been made; they are in the proceedings of the defence expenditures committee. No one can complain about dealing with matters of that kind. But I think it is a dangerous practice to take a position that is likely to make some sort of rift between our armed forces and the people of Canada which would be based on any misapprehension or misunderstanding of what are the real facts. I hope that when the committee on defence expenditures is reconstituted the facts that are brought out before that committee
will be put to more use by the members of the official opposition and not completely disregarded, as it is apparent they have disregarded the work done by the committee last session.
